title: Accidents and Illnesses
description: SPČR 2018 Exam Tests – diving accidents and illnesses, first aid, resuscitation

questions.question: When helping an unconscious casualty, the recommended first step is:

options.text: open the airway with a head tilt and check whether the casualty is breathing; if not, call EMS

questions.explanation: The first step is always to open the airway with a head tilt, check breathing, and call emergency medical services.

questions.question: What do you prioritise for an unconscious casualty bleeding heavily?
questions.explanation: Massive bleeding is life-threatening and must be controlled first, otherwise resuscitation will not be effective.

questions.question: Resuscitation is started when:

options.text: the casualty is unconscious and not breathing normally
the conscious casualty has no palpable pulse
the unconscious casualty has no palpable pulse
none of the answers is correct

questions.explanation: Resuscitation is started in an unconscious person who is not breathing normally. Pulse checks are no longer recommended for lay rescuers.

questions.question: The first action in resuscitation is:

options.text: opening the airway with a head tilt and checking whether the casualty is breathing; if not, calling EMS

questions.explanation: First open the airway, check breathing and call EMS, then start resuscitation.

questions.question: Lifting the casualty's lower limbs during resuscitation:

options.text: limits the effectiveness of chest compressions
limits the effectiveness of rescue breathing
is inadvisable because of the risk of blood pooling in the trunk

questions.explanation: Studies have shown that lifting the lower limbs during resuscitation provides no significant benefit.

questions.question: The site for chest compressions is:

options.text: approximately the middle of the chest, on the breastbone
in the left half of the chest
in the lower part of the chest, about three fingers below the breastbone
in the upper chest at the level of the collarbone joint

questions.explanation: The correct site is the middle of the chest on the breastbone, not on the left where the heart is.

questions.question: Chest compressions are performed at a rate of:
questions.explanation: Current resuscitation guidelines recommend 100–120 compressions per minute.

questions.question: Chest compressions:

options.text: are performed approximately in the middle of the chest, on the breastbone
are performed at a rate of about 100–120 per minute
are performed to a depth of 5–6 cm

questions.explanation: All of these are correct — middle of the chest, 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: During chest compressions, the chest is compressed at a rate of approximately 100–120 per minute.
The site for chest compressions is in the left half of the chest.
Chest compressions are performed to a depth of 5–6 cm.
Resuscitation begins with 30 chest compressions immediately after the airway is opened.

questions.explanation: Statement (b) is incorrect — the site for compressions is the middle of the chest on the breastbone, not the left half.

questions.question: During chest compressions, the casualty's chest is compressed:

options.text: approximately in the middle of the breastbone, to a depth of 5–6 cm
in the left part of the chest, at a rate of approximately 100–120 per minute
three fingers below the breastbone, at a rate of approximately 100–120 per minute, to a depth of 4–5 cm
approximately in the middle of the breastbone, at a rate of 70 per minute

questions.explanation: Compress the middle of the breastbone to a depth of 5–6 cm at 100–120/min.

questions.question: Adult resuscitation by a single rescuer requires:
questions.explanation: The standard adult ratio is 30:2 (30 compressions to 2 breaths), regardless of the number of rescuers.

questions.question: Adult resuscitation by two rescuers requires:
questions.explanation: For adults the ratio is always 30:2 regardless of whether one or two rescuers are working.

questions.question: Resuscitation after drowning requires:

options.text: first emptying water from the lungs
5 rescue breaths immediately after opening the airway
the rescuer(s) focusing only on chest compressions
only calling EMS, since lay first aid is impossible

questions.explanation: In drowning the priority is oxygenation, so we begin with 5 rescue breaths before starting compressions.

questions.question: The A-B-C resuscitation order (A = open airway, B = rescue breathing, C = chest compressions) is used:

options.text: in children from newborns to pre-school age
if the casualty is partly conscious

questions.explanation: The A-B-C order (breathing first) is used in children, where arrest is most often caused by oxygen deprivation rather than cardiac failure.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The first step in resuscitation is to open the casualty's airway.
Chest compressions are performed in cycles of 30.
The compression rate is 60–80 per minute.
If several rescuers are present, they should swap on chest compressions every 2 minutes.

questions.explanation: Statement (c) is incorrect — the correct rate is 100–120 per minute, not 60–80.

questions.question: The recovery position is:

options.text: any lying-down position on the ground
lying on the side with the head tilted back
lying on the back with the head supported

questions.explanation: The recovery position is on the side with the head tilted back, which allows fluids to drain from the mouth and keeps the airway clear.

questions.question: An unconscious casualty who is breathing:

options.text: is placed in the recovery position and covered to prevent cooling
is resuscitated with 15 chest compressions per 1 rescue breath
is placed on their back and EMS is called

questions.explanation: If an unconscious casualty is breathing, do not start resuscitation — place them in the recovery position and protect them from cooling.

questions.question: If the casualty is breathing but remains unconscious:

options.text: place them in the recovery position
continuously check that breathing has not stopped

questions.explanation: All these steps are correct — recovery position, continuous breathing check and protection from cooling.

questions.question: Covering a casualty placed in the recovery position:

options.text: is not recommended because it makes it harder to check the pulse
is not recommended because of the risk of overheating
is recommended to prevent heat loss
none of the answers is correct

questions.explanation: Covering the casualty is important to prevent hypothermia, which can worsen their condition.

questions.question: Each mouth-to-mouth rescue breath should last approximately:
questions.explanation: Each rescue breath should last about 1 second and should be enough to make the chest visibly rise.

questions.question: A hypothermia casualty is placed in a warm bath:

options.text: so that initially only the head is out of the water
so that initially only the trunk is submerged

questions.explanation: Warm only the trunk first so that cold blood from the limbs does not return to the heart too quickly and cause shock.

questions.question: Using compressed-air scuba, on reaching 40 m communication between you and your buddy worsens markedly. The cause should be considered:
questions.explanation: At 40 m the partial pressure of nitrogen is high enough to produce nitrogen narcosis, which impairs coordination and communication.

questions.question: When helping a hypothermic diver, it is appropriate to:
questions.explanation: Warm only the trunk. Massage and limb movement would push cold blood back to the heart and could trigger cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of hypothermia?

options.text: cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Cherry-red discolouration is a sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning, not hypothermia. In hypothermia the lips are blue.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: Hyperventilation lowers the carbon-dioxide level in the body.
The signs of oxygen deficiency (hypoxia) are hard to recognise.
Persistent pressure of equipment on the carotid arteries can reduce oxygen supply to the brain.
Hypoxia occurs when the partial pressure of oxygen in the breathing gas falls below 21 kPa.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — hypoxia occurs when pO₂ falls below about 16 kPa (0.16 bar), not 21 kPa. 21 kPa is the normal atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen.

questions.question: Hypoxia cannot result from:

options.text: binding of carbon monoxide to haemoglobin
breathing a 2% oxygen mixture at 90 m
breathing air stored long-term in a steel cylinder

questions.explanation: At 90 m the absolute pressure is 10 bar, so 2% O₂ gives pO₂ = 0.2 bar (20 kPa), which is sufficient and does not cause hypoxia.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement about nitrogen narcosis (rapture of the deep):

options.text: First aid is to ascend to a shallower depth.
The onset of narcosis is hastened by stress.
An oxygen-rebreather diver is not at risk of narcosis.
The narcotic effect of nitrogen can be reduced by increased physical exertion.

questions.explanation: Increased exertion in fact worsens narcosis because of CO₂ build-up, which amplifies the narcotic effect of nitrogen.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of hypoxia?
questions.explanation: Feeling unwell and nausea are not typical signs of hypoxia. Hypoxia presents with euphoria, increased heart and breathing rate, and impaired judgement.

questions.question: If your buddy shows signs of nitrogen narcosis:

options.text: you immediately make them ascend to a shallower depth
you immediately start an emergency ascent to the surface
you stay together at the same depth until the symptoms pass
you continue descending until the symptoms pass

questions.explanation: The correct first aid for narcosis is to ascend to a shallower depth, where the narcotic effect of nitrogen quickly subsides.

questions.question: The narcotic effect of nitrogen is amplified by:
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) amplifies the narcotic effect of nitrogen. That is why proper breathing technique and avoiding exertion at depth matter.

questions.question: Hypoxia is a risk:

options.text: on a breath-hold dive after hyperventilation
if the regulator is removed in dry pockets sealed underwater

questions.explanation: All these can cause hypoxia — hyperventilation lowers CO₂ and suppresses the breathing reflex, sealed pockets have limited oxygen, and long-stored air can have its oxygen consumed by reaction with the steel walls.

questions.question: A breathing mixture contains 4% oxygen. It can be used without risk of hypoxia only at depths greater than:
questions.explanation: Safe breathing requires pO₂ of at least 0.16 bar. At 30 m (4 bar) we get 4% × 4 = 0.16 bar (16 kPa), which is the minimum safe value.

questions.question: Loss of consciousness is a risk when the partial pressure of oxygen in the breathing gas drops below:
questions.explanation: Loss of consciousness is a risk when pO₂ falls below 10 kPa (0.1 bar). 16 kPa is the minimum for normal function; below 10 kPa, consciousness is lost.

questions.question: Using air stored long-term (e.g. several months) in a steel cylinder may lead to:
questions.explanation: Oxygen in long-stored air can react with the steel cylinder walls (oxidation/rust), reducing its content and creating a hypoxia risk.

questions.question: Hypoxia occurs when the partial pressure of oxygen in the breathing gas drops below:
questions.explanation: Hypoxia occurs when pO₂ falls below 16 kPa (0.16 bar). This is the minimum partial pressure of oxygen needed for normal body function.

questions.question: The appropriate temperature of a shower or bath for a hypothermic diver is approximately:
questions.explanation: The optimal warming temperature is 37–40 °C — close to body temperature, so it does not cause thermal shock.

questions.question: When helping a hypothermic diver, the priority is:
questions.explanation: In hypothermia the priority is to warm the trunk, where the vital organs are. Warming the limbs can push cold blood back to the heart.

questions.question: When helping a hypothermic diver it is appropriate to:

options.text: wrap the casualty in pre-warmed blankets

questions.explanation: All of these are appropriate ways of warming a hypothermic diver — pre-warmed blankets, a warm bath and a warm shower.

questions.question: In hypothermia it is inappropriate to:

options.text: warm the casualty with a warm shower or bath
warm the casualty with the rescuer's body heat

questions.explanation: Exercising a hypothermic casualty is inappropriate, because limb movement speeds the return of cold peripheral blood to the heart and can cause cardiac arrhythmia.

questions.question: Uncontrolled shivering:

options.text: is a normal effect of being in water and need not be addressed
is a serious sign of hypothermia
is not a risk for a diver in a full insulating suit
precedes the first signs of hypothermia

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled shivering is a serious sign of hypothermia and requires immediate attention and rewarming.

questions.question: Cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Cyanosis (bluish discolouration) of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of carbon-dioxide toxicity, caused by inadequate blood oxygenation.

questions.question: A characteristic sign of carbon-dioxide toxicity is:

options.text: cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Cyanosis is the characteristic sign of CO₂ toxicity. Cherry-red discolouration is typical of carbon-monoxide poisoning.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of carbon-dioxide toxicity?

options.text: cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Muscle and joint pain is a sign of decompression sickness, not carbon-dioxide toxicity.

questions.question: Carbon-dioxide toxicity cannot result from:

options.text: excessive exertion on a scuba dive

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ in the body, so it cannot cause CO₂ toxicity. Excessive exertion and improper breathing, by contrast, cause CO₂ build-up.

questions.question: Carbon-dioxide toxicity can be caused by:

options.text: contamination of the air supply with exhaust fumes
persistent pressure of equipment on the carotid arteries

questions.explanation: An unsuitable snorkel (too long or too narrow) increases dead space and traps exhaled CO₂, leading to toxicity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of acute oxygen toxicity?

options.text: twitching of small muscles in the hands and face

questions.explanation: Headache is not a typical sign of acute oxygen toxicity. Typical signs include muscle twitching, convulsions and loss of consciousness.

questions.question: Cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Cyanosis (bluish discolouration) of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of carbon-dioxide toxicity, which results in inadequate blood oxygenation.

questions.question: A characteristic sign of carbon-dioxide toxicity is:

options.text: cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Cyanosis is the characteristic sign of CO₂ toxicity, because it leads to insufficient blood oxygenation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning?

options.text: cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Stabbing pain behind the breastbone is not a typical sign of CO poisoning. Typical signs include headache, dizziness, nausea and cherry-red discolouration.

questions.question: Acute oxygen toxicity on compressed-air scuba is a risk from approximately:
questions.explanation: On air (21% O₂) the oxygen partial pressure reaches the toxic threshold of 1.6 bar at approximately 70 m (8 bar × 0.21 = 1.68 bar).

questions.question: A characteristic sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning is:

options.text: cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Cherry-red discolouration is characteristic of CO poisoning, because carboxyhaemoglobin (CO bound to haemoglobin) is bright red.

questions.question: Carbon-monoxide poisoning can be caused by:

options.text: persistent pressure of equipment on the carotid arteries
contamination of the air supply with exhaust fumes
an elevated partial pressure of nitrogen

questions.explanation: Contamination of the air supply with exhaust fumes is the main cause of CO poisoning in diving — exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide.

questions.question: Acute oxygen toxicity presents with:

options.text: cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
twitching of small muscles, violent convulsions, loss of consciousness

questions.explanation: Acute oxygen toxicity (Paul Bert effect) presents with muscle twitching, violent convulsions and subsequent loss of consciousness.

questions.question: The basis of carbon-monoxide poisoning is:

options.text: dissolution of carbon monoxide in the tissues
dissolution of carbon monoxide in blood plasma
chemical binding of carbon monoxide to blood plasma
chemical binding of carbon monoxide to haemoglobin

questions.explanation: CO binds to haemoglobin with an affinity 200–250× greater than oxygen, blocking oxygen transport in the blood and causing tissue hypoxia.

questions.question: A characteristic sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning is:

options.text: cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Cherry-red discolouration is typical of CO poisoning because of the bright red colour of carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood.

questions.question: Cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Cherry-red discolouration is a typical sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning, where CO binds to haemoglobin and produces this characteristic colour.

questions.question: Acute oxygen toxicity is a risk if the oxygen partial pressure in the breathing gas exceeds approximately:
questions.explanation: Acute oxygen toxicity (hyperoxia) is a risk above 160 kPa (1.6 bar), which is the safety limit for diving.

questions.question: Cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Cherry-red discolouration is a characteristic sign of carbon-monoxide poisoning because carboxyhaemoglobin is markedly red.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: Carbon monoxide blocks oxygen transport by binding to haemoglobin.
CO poisoning during diving is caused by contamination of the air supply with exhaust fumes.
CO poisoning includes headache, dizziness, nausea and vomiting.
A characteristic sign of CO poisoning is cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — carbon-monoxide poisoning produces cherry-red discolouration, not cyanosis. Cyanosis is characteristic of carbon-dioxide toxicity.

questions.question: Carbon-dioxide toxicity can result from:
questions.explanation: All these can lead to CO₂ toxicity — an unsuitable snorkel with large dead space, exertion increasing CO₂ production, and improper breathing technique.

questions.question: On descent on compressed-air scuba, at 15 m your buddy starts to show signs of disorientation, spinning around and struggling with motor coordination. The cause is:
questions.explanation: Disorientation and motor coordination problems on descent at shallow depth point to inner-ear damage — a ruptured eardrum causes vertigo and loss of orientation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: Paralysis is not a sign of pneumothorax. Pneumothorax presents with chest pain, cough and distended neck veins. Paralysis is more characteristic of decompression sickness or arterial gas embolism.

questions.question: Mask squeeze (eye barotrauma):

options.text: cannot occur because the eyeball is filled with vitreous humour
cannot occur because the eye equalises pressure differences by its own elasticity
can occur if the diver does not equalise pressure in the mask on descent
can occur if the diver does not equalise pressure in the mask on ascent

questions.explanation: Mask squeeze can occur on descent if the diver does not equalise the pressure inside the mask by exhaling through the nose. Negative pressure in the mask can damage the eyes and cause bleeding.

questions.question: Pulmonary barotrauma of descent (lung squeeze) presents with:

options.text: pain at the bridge of the nose and below the eyes
chest pain, sometimes with coughing of pinkish foam
cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Lung squeeze presents with chest pain and coughing of pinkish foam — blood mixed with air from damaged alveoli.

questions.question: In diving, emphysema occurs when air from a ruptured lung enters:

options.text: the mediastinum or the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders

questions.explanation: Emphysema occurs when air enters the mediastinum (mediastinal emphysema) or the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders (subcutaneous emphysema). Air in the bloodstream is an embolism; air in the pleural space is pneumothorax.

questions.question: On scuba, pulmonary barotrauma of descent (lung squeeze):

options.text: is a risk after losing control of breathing during a fall to depth
is a risk when lifting heavier objects by hand
is a risk on ascent without exhaling

questions.explanation: Pulmonary barotrauma of descent is a risk during a rapid fall to depth, when the diver loses control of breathing and cannot supply enough air to the lungs.

questions.question: Pain at the bridge of the nose and below the eyes is a sign of:
questions.explanation: Pain at the bridge of the nose and below the eyes is a typical sign of sinus barotrauma.

questions.question: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent on scuba can occur on an incorrectly performed ascent from a depth as shallow as:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent can occur at very shallow depths (less than 2 m), because the relative pressure change is greatest near the surface.

questions.question: Tooth squeeze (barodontalgia):

options.text: is impossible because of tooth structure
can only occur on dives below 40 m
is painful and can be dangerous, especially on ascent

questions.explanation: Tooth squeeze is painful and can be dangerous, especially on ascent, when air trapped in tooth cavities expands.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of arterial gas embolism?
questions.explanation: Muscle and joint pain is a sign of decompression sickness, not arterial gas embolism. AGE presents with neurological signs.

questions.question: In diving, pneumothorax occurs when air from a ruptured lung enters:

options.text: the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders

questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is caused by air entering the pleural space, which causes the lung to collapse.

questions.question: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent on scuba can occur on an incorrectly performed ascent from a depth as shallow as:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent can occur at depths less than 2 m, because the relative pressure change is greatest near the surface.

questions.question: Inner-ear damage from over-pressure:

options.text: cannot occur because the inner ear is separated from the middle ear by bone
cannot occur because inner-ear organs are filled with fluid
can occur on attempts at forceful equalisation of the middle ear

questions.explanation: Inner-ear damage can occur during a forceful Valsalva manoeuvre, where over-pressure in the middle ear damages the oval or round window.

questions.question: The vertigo on a ruptured eardrum underwater is mainly caused by:

options.text: sudden cooling of the inner ear by water entering the middle-ear cavity

questions.explanation: The vertigo on a ruptured eardrum is caused by sudden cooling of the inner ear by cold water entering the middle-ear cavity.

questions.question: In diving, arterial gas embolism (AGE) is caused by air from a ruptured lung entering:

options.text: the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders

questions.explanation: Arterial gas embolism is caused by air bubbles from a ruptured lung entering the bloodstream directly.

questions.question: The consequences of pulmonary barotrauma of ascent appear:

options.text: between 30 minutes and 3 hours after surfacing
between 30 minutes and 1 hour after surfacing
immediately on surfacing, or even during the ascent

questions.explanation: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent is an acute injury whose signs (embolism, pneumothorax, emphysema) appear immediately on ascent or surfacing.

questions.question: Arterial gas embolism is a consequence of:
questions.explanation: Arterial gas embolism is caused by air entering the bloodstream from a ruptured lung — a consequence of pulmonary barotrauma of ascent.

questions.question: Pneumothorax is a consequence of:
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is caused by air entering the pleural space from a ruptured lung — a consequence of pulmonary barotrauma of ascent.

questions.question: The cause of pulmonary barotrauma of ascent is:

options.text: tissue super-saturation with nitrogen on ascent on scuba
breath-holding on ascent during a breath-hold dive
insufficient exhalation, or breath-holding on ascent on scuba

questions.explanation: Pulmonary barotrauma of ascent occurs on a scuba ascent when the diver does not exhale enough or holds their breath — air in the lungs expands and can rupture lung tissue.

questions.question: Air entering the mediastinum, or the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders, is called:
questions.explanation: Emphysema (mediastinal or subcutaneous) is the entry of air from a ruptured lung into the mediastinum or into the subcutaneous tissue around the neck and shoulders.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: Decompression sickness does not occur in divers who do not exceed the no-decompression limit for a given depth.
Cutaneous DCS does not require recompression-chamber treatment.
The partial pressure of oxygen breathed during in-water decompression must not exceed 170 kPa.
A surface interval longer than 2 hours is recommended.

questions.explanation: This statement is incorrect — DCS can occur even within no-decompression limits, especially on repetitive dives or in the presence of risk factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of decompression sickness?

options.text: pain at the bridge of the nose and below the eyes

questions.explanation: Pain at the bridge of the nose and below the eyes is a sign of sinus barotrauma, not decompression sickness.

questions.question: Pulmonary DCS (the chokes):

options.text: is accompanied by muscle and joint pain
is caused by nitrogen bubbles blocking pulmonary capillaries

questions.explanation: Pulmonary DCS (the chokes) is caused by nitrogen bubbles blocking pulmonary capillaries, which interferes with respiratory-gas exchange.

questions.question: In a case of decompression sickness, it is NOT recommended to:
questions.explanation: Analgesics can mask the signs of DCS and complicate diagnosis. Oxygen, rest and professional evaluation are the recommended steps.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: All forms of decompression sickness require recompression-chamber treatment.
The musculoskeletal form is the most common form of DCS.
Cutaneous DCS is caused by nitrogen bubbles blocking skin capillaries.
Most cases of DCS appear from 30 minutes to 3 hours after surfacing.

questions.explanation: This statement is incorrect — cutaneous DCS does not normally require recompression-chamber treatment, only observation and conservative management.

questions.question: Pulmonary DCS:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary DCS blocks gas exchange, threatens the heart and requires immediate chamber treatment — all answers are correct.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of musculoskeletal DCS?

options.text: holding the limbs in a flexed position

questions.explanation: Pain behind the breastbone is a sign of pulmonary DCS, not musculoskeletal DCS.

questions.question: Recompression-chamber treatment is required for:
questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal DCS requires recompression-chamber treatment. Cutaneous and lymphatic forms are milder and do not require chamber treatment.

questions.question: Pulmonary DCS:

options.text: is caused by nitrogen bubbles inside the alveoli

questions.explanation: Pulmonary DCS can lead to cardiac failure because nitrogen bubbles block the pulmonary capillaries.

questions.question: Which form of DCS does NOT require recompression-chamber treatment?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic DCS is a mild form that does not require recompression-chamber treatment.

questions.question: The most serious form of DCS is:
questions.explanation: Neurological DCS affects the central nervous system and can cause paralysis or death, making it the most serious form.

questions.question: Paralysis is a sign of:
questions.explanation: Paralysis is a characteristic sign of neurological DCS, which affects the spinal cord and brain.

questions.question: DCS most often presents as:
questions.explanation: The musculoskeletal form (joint and muscle pain — the bends) is the most common form of decompression sickness.

questions.question: A characteristic sign of cutaneous DCS is:

options.text: cyanosis of the lips, mucosae and nail beds
cherry-red discolouration of the lips, mucosae and nail beds

questions.explanation: Skin mottling (cutis marmorata) is a typical sign of cutaneous DCS.

questions.question: Shallow breathing, breathlessness and stabbing pain behind the breastbone are signs of:
questions.explanation: These signs are typical of pulmonary DCS, caused by bubbles blocking the pulmonary capillaries.

questions.question: Skin mottling is a sign of:
questions.explanation: Skin mottling is a characteristic sign of cutaneous decompression sickness.

questions.question: Musculoskeletal DCS:

options.text: makes the casualty hold their limbs in a flexed position
tolerates a longer transport to the recompression chamber

questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal DCS has all these features — flexed posture eases the pain, it requires chamber treatment, but it tolerates a longer transport.

questions.question: DCS signs appear:

options.text: immediately on surfacing (or even during the ascent)
often only on the shore or boat, sometimes hours later

questions.explanation: DCS signs often appear after surfacing — typically from 30 minutes to several hours after the dive.

questions.question: The risk of decompression incidents is increased by:
questions.explanation: Physical exertion and cooling increase the risk of DCS by impairing tissue off-gassing.

questions.question: Replacing nitrogen in the breathing gas with helium eliminates:
questions.explanation: Helium has no narcotic effect like nitrogen, so its use eliminates nitrogen narcosis.
